theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A school board in May Pen asks your firm to "sort out the electrics" in a classroom block. What should the planner do first?

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters CPM stand for in job planning?
Tasks of 3 days and 4 days run one after the other, and a 5-day task runs alongside them. How many days does the job take?
Materials cost J$95 000 and labour J$65 000. The firm adds 10% for overheads and profit. What is the price before GCT, in J$?
Which test instrument must be booked for the dead test of insulation between conductors and earth?
What is the name of the stage when old wiring and fittings are taken out before a rewire?
What is the name of the document that records the test results and states that a new installation is safe to use?
A task on the critical path finishes 2 days late, and every other task is on time. By how many days does the finish date move?
Twelve rooms are planned evenly over 6 days. By the end of day 4, how many rooms should be finished?
An inspection is booked for Friday 12 June 2026. Testing takes 2 working days and must end the day before. On which day of the week must testing start?
Wiring 24 outlets costs J$156 000 in all. What is the cost per outlet, in J$?
Labour costs J$2 200 an hour and a job needs 45 labour-hours. What is the labour cost, in J$?
What two-word phrase names the useful points a team writes down after a job so the next one goes better?
From the drawings, the planner counts every box, metre of cable and fitting. What is this list called?
How many working days (Monday to Friday) are there from Monday 1 June to Friday 19 June 2026, counting both days?
A 3-day task can start on day 4 at the earliest and has 2 days of float. What is the latest day it can start without delaying the job?

essays.stem: A school in May Pen wants a four-classroom block rewired during term time. Explain how you would plan the job from the first request to the start of work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would meet the principal to agree a written scope: which rooms, what the new installation includes, the standard and drawings it must meet, and the date it must be ready for inspection. I would survey the block, checking the existing board, earthing, routes, ceiling condition and any hazards such as possible asbestos. I would break the work into tasks: strip-out, first fix, second fix, testing and handover for each room, and set the order so only one or two rooms are out of use at a time, fitted around the school timetable and exams. I would estimate labour and materials, order long-lead items such as the new board early, and plan temporary supplies for essential loads. I would write the risk assessment and isolation plan, plan how pupils are kept away from the work, prepare a bar chart, and get the plan approved by my supervisor and the school.
markingPoints: Agrees a written scope with the school, including standard and date
Surveys the building and records hazards
Breaks work into tasks and sequences rooms around the timetable
Estimates labour and materials; orders long-lead items; temporary supplies
Risk assessment, isolation plan, pupil safety, bar chart and approval

essays.stem: A shop fit-out has these tasks: A survey and design (2 days); B order and receive board (6 days, after A); C first fix (5 days, after A); D second fix (3 days, after B and C); E testing (1 day, after D); F handover (1 day, after E). Find the critical path, the job length and the float on C, and explain what these mean for the planner.
essays.modelAnswer: After A ends on day 2, B and C both start. B takes 6 days, ending on day 8. C takes 5 days, ending on day 7. D needs both, so it starts after day 8 and ends on day 11. E ends on day 12 and F on day 13. The critical path is A, B, D, E, F, and the job takes 13 days. C has 1 day of float, because it ends on day 7 but D cannot start until day 8. This means any delay to the board order, or to A, D, E or F, delays the whole job, so the planner must order the board the moment the design is fixed and chase the supplier. C can slip by up to one day without harm, so its electricians could help elsewhere for a day if needed. If the board could be delivered sooner, the job would shorten until C became critical.
markingPoints: Works out task timings correctly
Critical path A–B–D–E–F
Job length 13 days
Float on C is 1 day, with the reason
Explains what it means: watch and chase B; use C's float; shortening B shortens the job

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the isolation and temporary supplies for rewiring part of a working guest house, so guests and staff are safe and essential services stay on.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list what each circuit feeds, using the board chart and tests, and find the essential loads, such as kitchen fridges, water pumps, security lights and alarms. I would plan the work in stages so only the circuits being worked on are off, and agree the times with the manager so guests are told in advance. Where an essential load is on a circuit we must work on, I would plan a temporary supply from another protected circuit or a suitable temporary board, installed and tested properly, not a trailing lead across walkways. For each stage, the plan says which circuits are isolated, by whom, where locks and tags go, and that each circuit is proved dead with a tester checked before and after. It also covers how supplies are restored only after tests and with every lock removed by its owner. Finally I would brief the team and the staff.
markingPoints: Identifies what each circuit feeds and the essential loads
Works in stages; agrees times; guests told in advance
Safe, tested temporary supplies for essential loads
States who isolates, lock and tag, prove dead with tester checked before and after
Restoring supply after tests and lock removal; briefs team and staff

essays.stem: A small business wants a standby generator connected to its building. Describe what your plan must cover.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan starts by listing the loads the generator must run, so it can be sized correctly, allowing for motor starting. It must include a changeover switch that disconnects the mains before connecting the generator, so the generator can never feed back into the public lines and endanger linesmen. The generator's position must be outdoors or in a ventilated enclosure, with the exhaust well away from doors and windows because of carbon monoxide, and protected from rain and flooding. The plan covers fuel storage, fire safety and noise for neighbours. It sets out the cable sizes, protection, earthing arrangement and the location of an emergency stop. It includes the isolation plan for connecting to the existing board, the tests and the inspection needed, and training the owner to start, stop and change over safely. It also lists the maker's instructions to follow.
markingPoints: Lists loads and sizes the generator
Changeover switch to prevent back-feed into public lines
Safe location: ventilation, exhaust away from openings, weather and flooding
Fuel, fire, noise, cables, protection, earthing and emergency stop
Isolation for connection, tests, inspection and owner training

essays.stem: Explain how you would build quality checks and tests into the plan for an electrical installation, from first fix to handover.
essays.modelAnswer: I would list in the plan every check, when it happens and who signs it. At first fix, the team leader checks routes, box positions and heights, cable sizes, supports and segregation against the drawings, room by room. A hold point is placed before walls and ceilings are closed, so concealed cables can be inspected and photographed. At second fix, the leader checks that accessories are level, terminations tight and earths connected. Then the dead tests are planned: continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance, polarity, and the other tests the standard requires, with results recorded. After the supply is restored by the authorised person, function tests and GFCI or RCD tests follow. The plan also books the government electrical inspection in time for the power company to connect. Finally, a snag list is cleared and the test certificate and records are handed over.
markingPoints: Lists checks, timing and who signs
First fix checks against drawings, room by room
Hold point before walls and ceilings are closed
Second fix checks; dead tests recorded; function and GFCI or RCD tests after energising
Government inspection booked; snag list; certificate and records at handover

essays.stem: Describe how you would monitor a three-week electrical job against its plan, and what you would do if it fell three days behind.
essays.modelAnswer: I would keep the bar chart on site and mark progress on it every day, comparing what was done with what was planned. A short daily diary would record work done, people on site, deliveries, problems and who was told. Each week I would report to my supervisor with the percentage complete and any risks. If the job fell three days behind, I would first find the cause, for example a late delivery, extra work or too few people. I would check whether the delayed tasks are on the critical path; if they are not and have enough float, the finish date may not move. If they are, I would look at options with my supervisor: adding people, working extra hours safely, changing the order of tasks or using float elsewhere. I would agree the new plan, tell the customer honestly about any change to the finish date, and update the chart.
markingPoints: Marks progress on the bar chart daily; compares with plan
Keeps a site diary and reports weekly
Finds the cause of the delay
Checks the critical path and float; considers recovery options
Agrees the new plan, informs the customer and updates the chart

essays.stem: Explain how you would prepare a cost estimate for rewiring a small house in Old Harbour, and how you would present it to the customer.
essays.modelAnswer: From the drawing or survey I would make a take-off of all materials: cable by size, boxes, accessories, the board and breakers, conduit and fixings, with an allowance for waste. I would price these from current supplier quotes. I would estimate labour from past jobs, for example the hours per outlet or light, add time for strip-out, testing and making good, and multiply by the labour rate. I would add the cost of hire items, transport and waste disposal, then a contingency for hidden problems in an old house, and the firm's overheads and profit. GCT is added at the current rate on a separate line. I would present the estimate in writing, in plain words, listing what is included and excluded, how long the price is valid, the payment terms and the expected time on site. I would explain it to the customer and answer questions before they sign.
markingPoints: Take-off of materials with waste allowance, priced from current quotes
Labour estimated from past records and multiplied by the rate
Hire, transport, disposal, contingency, overheads and profit
GCT shown separately at the current rate
Clear written estimate with inclusions, exclusions, validity, terms and time; explained to the customer

essays.stem: Explain how you would coordinate an electrical job with other trades, such as plumbers, air-conditioning installers, ceiling fixers and painters, on a building site.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts I would go through the drawings with the main contractor and the other trades to agree routes and spaces, so ducts, pipes and cables do not clash. I would agree the order of work: for example, our first fix must be done before ceilings and walls are closed, and our second fix after painting. I would put these links into the programme so everyone sees when they depend on each other. I would attend site meetings, share our programme and tell others early if our work is late or if their work holds us up. On site I would agree shared hazards, such as hot work, ladders and open ceilings, and who isolates which supplies. Any change agreed with another trade would be written down and marked on the drawings. Good coordination saves rework and keeps everyone safe.
markingPoints: Reviews drawings with other trades to avoid clashes
Agrees the order of work and links it in the programme
Attends meetings and gives early warning of delays
Agrees shared hazards and isolation responsibilities
Records agreed changes; explains the benefit

essays.stem: Halfway through a job, the customer asks for two extra 220 V circuits for air-conditioning units. Explain how you would deal with the request.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank the customer and explain that I must check the request before agreeing. First I would check the design: the new load, whether the board has spare ways, whether the supply and main cable can carry the extra current, and the cable sizes and protection the units' nameplates require. If the supply or board is too small, that must be raised, because it may need the power company or a larger board. Then I would work out the extra materials, labour, time and cost, and see how it affects the programme and the critical path. I would put this in a written variation for the customer to sign before the extra work starts. I would update the drawings, the circuit schedule, the materials list and the bar chart, and brief the team. The new circuits are tested and recorded with the rest.
markingPoints: Checks the design: load, spare ways, supply and main cable capacity, nameplate needs
Raises any supply or board upgrade needed
Works out extra materials, labour, time, cost and effect on programme
Written variation signed before work starts
Updates drawings, schedules and chart; briefs team; tests and records

essays.stem: Explain how a bar chart and a network diagram can be used together to plan and control an electrical job. Give a short example.
essays.modelAnswer: A network diagram shows each task as a box joined by arrows to the tasks that must come before and after it. From it, the planner finds the critical path, the job length and the float on each task. A bar chart then shows the same tasks as bars along a calendar, so everyone can see what happens each day and which tasks overlap. For example, in a small office job, the network shows that first fix and ordering the board both follow the survey, and second fix needs both. If the board takes longer, it is on the critical path. The bar chart then places these tasks on dates, shows the people needed each day, and marks hold points and the inspection date. During the job the bar chart is used to mark progress daily, and the network is used to check whether a delay will move the finish date.
markingPoints: Network diagram shows dependencies; gives critical path and float
Bar chart shows tasks on a calendar and overlaps
Gives a relevant electrical example
Uses the bar chart for daily progress and resources
Uses the network to judge the effect of delays

practical1.title: Prepare a complete job plan for rewiring a classroom block
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a pack for an imaginary job: drawings of a four-classroom block, the school's timetable, a price list, supplier lead times and a labour rate. As a planning team, produce a complete job plan: (1) a written scope agreed with the assessor acting as the principal; (2) a breakdown of tasks with times; (3) a network diagram with the critical path and float marked; (4) a bar chart showing tasks, dates, people and hold points; (5) a materials take-off with order dates; (6) a cost estimate with overheads, contingency and GCT shown as a separate line at the rate the assessor gives; (7) a risk assessment and an isolation and temporary supply plan that keeps pupils safe; and (8) a quality and test plan up to the government inspection. Each member leads one or two parts and checks another member's part. The group then presents the plan to the assessor, and every member answers questions on their part. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan.
materials: Job pack from the assessor: drawings, timetable, price list, lead times and labour rate
Planning forms: task list, take-off sheet, estimate sheet, risk assessment, isolation plan, test plan
Graph paper or a computer with a spreadsheet for the bar chart
Flip chart and markers for the network diagram
photos: The network diagram with the critical path marked
The bar chart with hold points
The risk assessment and isolation plan
checklist: Helped agree a clear, measurable scope
Led a part of the plan and made it complete and accurate
Worked out the critical path, job length and float correctly
Set order dates that meet the programme, using the lead times
Included safe isolation (lock, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after) and temporary supplies in the plan
Checked another member's part and corrected errors
Explained their part clearly and answered questions
safety: This is a planning task: no tools or supplies are used
Plan every task so that no work is done live
Include pupil and public safety in every stage of the plan
Keep the room tidy and cables from laptops off the floor

practical2.title: Plan, carry out, track and review a small installation on a training bay
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing for a small installation on a training bay: one lighting circuit with two lights and a switch, and one outlet circuit with two outlets, fed from a small board. The bay is not connected to any supply. First, plan the job: tasks, times, a bar chart with hold points, a materials list, a risk assessment and who does what. Show the plan to the assessor before you start. Then carry out the work, marking actual progress on the bar chart every 30 minutes. Halfway through, the assessor will give the group a change (for example, an extra outlet). Work out its effect on time and materials, write a short variation, get it approved, and update the bar chart. Stop at each hold point for the assessor's check. Finish with dead tests (protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance, polarity), record the results, and hand over to the assessor with a circuit chart. Last, hold a short review and write what went well, what did not, and what you would change next time. Each member leads at least one task and takes part in the review. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan, the marked-up chart, the variation, the test results and the review.
materials: Training bay with a small board (not connected to any supply)
Cable, boxes, switch, outlets, lamp holders, fixings and containment
Hand tools, drill, level and tape measure
Low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
Planning forms, bar chart sheet, variation form, test record, circuit chart and review sheet
photos: The plan and bar chart before work starts
Work under way, with progress marked on the chart
The variation form, approved, and the updated chart
The first fix at the hold point
The dead tests and the test record
checklist: Helped make a realistic plan with times, hold points and roles
Led at least one task and kept to the plan or reported why not
Marked progress honestly and on time
Worked out the effect of the change and updated the plan
Stopped at hold points and acted on the assessor's checks
Carried out or checked dead tests and recorded them
Gave useful points in the review
safety: The bay is never connected to a supply during the task
Wear safety glasses when drilling and cutting
Check power tools and leads before use, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep the work area tidy, with off-cuts picked up as you go
